title: Lookup no longer returns ErrNotFound, breaking errors.Is checks by callers
rationale: The still-exported ErrNotFound sentinel documents that not-found is reported via that error, but Lookup now returns an error that does not wrap it. Any caller branching with errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) will silently fail to detect missing users. Either wrap the sentinel (fmt.Errorf("user %q: %w", id, ErrNotFound)) or remove the exported sentinel; both cannot stand as they are.

title: Unit change to seconds breaks the unchanged caller, which passes the value to AbortSignal.timeout (milliseconds)
rationale: fetchWithTimeout feeds the result straight into AbortSignal.timeout, which interprets its argument as milliseconds; with the new seconds unit a configured "30s" timeout now aborts after 30 ms and a "1500ms" one after 1.5 ms, failing essentially every request. Either revert to milliseconds here or scale by 1000 at the unchanged call site.

title: Lookup no longer returns ErrNotFound, breaking errors.Is checks
rationale: Callers use errors.Is(err, store.ErrNotFound) to map missing users to a 404, but the sentinel has been replaced with a plain fmt.Errorf with no %w, so every unknown-id request falls through to the generic error branch and returns a 500 instead of a 404.

title: Stale comment on ErrNotFound
rationale: The comment still documents that Lookup returns ErrNotFound, but the implementation no longer does; the next caller written against the comment will repeat the 500-instead-of-404 mistake.

title: Lookup no longer returns ErrNotFound, breaking errors.Is callers
rationale: Lookup no longer returns ErrNotFound, so the caller's errors.Is(err, store.ErrNotFound) check at web/users.go:17 never matches; unknown ids now return a plain fmt.Errorf and get a 500 instead of 404. Wrapping with %w preserves the contract.

title: parseDuration's return unit changes from milliseconds to seconds, changing the contract for every caller
rationale: For the same input the function now returns a value 1000x smaller ("2s" returns 2 instead of 2000), and ms inputs can be fractional ("1500ms" returns 1.5). This breaks the previous milliseconds contract for any caller not migrated in this change; the callers were not shown, so the impact rests on the assumption that some call site still expects milliseconds.

title: Negative limit bypasses the MAX_PAGE guard
rationale: The check only rejects limit > MAX_PAGE, so a negative limit such as -1 passes; in SQLite, a negative LIMIT means no upper bound, returning the entire table — precisely what the new docstring claims the guard prevents. Negative values are a common 'unbounded' idiom or arise from arithmetic on page sizes, so this silently defeats the check.

title: Remaining() now returns megabytes while the rest of the type's API is specified in bytes
rationale: New and Record operate in bytes, so the type's API now mixes units across identically-typed int64 values; a caller comparing Remaining() to a byte count or feeding its result back into Record compiles cleanly and is wrong by a factor of 2^20. Because limit and used are unexported, callers outside the package also lose any way to obtain byte-precision remaining at all. Converting to megabytes at the dashboard call site, or renaming the method to make the unit explicit (e.g. RemainingMB), would keep the units unambiguous.

title: Remaining() changes units from bytes to megabytes, breaking the method's contract for existing callers
rationale: Remaining() previously returned bytes; dividing by 1<<20 changes the value by a factor of 1,048,576, so any caller still comparing the result against byte counts now gets wrong answers, and a tenant with less than 1 MB left reports 0 while still able to upload. If the dashboard needs megabytes, expose a separate method and keep Remaining()'s byte semantics.

title: Remaining() now returns megabytes, but the upload handler compares it against a byte count
rationale: web/upload.go:22 compares h.Quota.Remaining() against int64(len(body)), pitting megabytes against bytes: with a 64 MB quota and no usage, Remaining() returns 64 and every upload larger than 64 bytes is rejected with 413 despite ample quota remaining. Keep Remaining() returning bytes and convert to megabytes at the dashboard call site, or add a separate megabyte accessor.

title: Lookup no longer returns the documented ErrNotFound sentinel
rationale: Lookup previously returned ErrNotFound (documented on line 8); it now returns a fresh fmt.Errorf, so any caller doing errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) or err == ErrNotFound will treat a missing user as an unexpected failure. The sentinel variable and its doc comment are still exported, which further advertises a contract that is no longer honored.

title: Exported parseDuration now returns seconds instead of milliseconds, changing the value every existing caller sees
rationale: The exported function's documented return unit flips from milliseconds to seconds, and both are plain `number`, so the type system will not flag any caller still written against the old contract; such a caller gets durations short by 1000x (60x for minutes). The docstring update shows the change is deliberate, but it is only safe if every caller is updated in this same change, which the shown code does not demonstrate.

title: Remaining() now returns megabytes, silently breaking the byte-based quota check in web/upload.go
rationale: The upload handler compares Remaining() against int64(len(body)) in bytes, so after this change a tenant with 100 MB (104857600 bytes) remaining gets Remaining() == 100 and the handler rejects any upload larger than 100 bytes with 413, even though the quota allows it. Keep Remaining() in bytes and format megabytes at the dashboard, or add a separate RemainingMB() for display, rather than changing the unit of an existing method under its callers.

title: Switching the return unit to seconds breaks the existing caller, which feeds the value to AbortSignal.timeout (milliseconds)
rationale: If src/http.ts passes parseDuration's result straight to AbortSignal.timeout (milliseconds), the new seconds semantics make a configured "30s" timeout abort after 30 ms, so every request through fetchWithTimeout fails almost immediately. The caller is not shown, so this rests on the caller feeding the value unconverted to a millisecond-based API; if confirmed, the fix is to keep the millisecond contract or convert (×1000) at the caller.
